title: Why I'm posting for 20 days
post:
Over the past 5-6 months I’ve built 20 products. In September I left my job to build full time.
Now I’m looking for my next role in product and AI, and for 20 days I’ll share one build a day.

The roles I’m after: Product Lead, AI Product Manager or Forward Deployed Engineer. Somewhere product and AI meet, and I can shape the product and also build it hands-on with customers.

Before building full time, I spent close to 4 years at Times Internet, growing from APM to Senior PM:
• Led the discovery, registration and acquisition journeys for the inaugural Times Internet Delhi Half Marathon: 18K+ runners
• Launched paid wellness subscriptions for Times Health+
• Scaled The Economic Times’ Assisted Sales revenue from ₹15L to ₹80L a month, and built AI TeleSuite for that team
• Drove ₹3Cr+ in incremental ARR at ET Markets

Most recently, I was AGM, Product Management, running D2C growth across the US, UK and global markets.

Why a series and not just a CV? A CV tells you what someone did. It doesn’t show how they think. So each post covers one build: the problem, the insight, the decisions I made and the trade-offs I accepted.

Building 20 products taught me five things you’ll see again and again:
1. Trust is a feature. You’ll meet a disaster map that tells you when it was wrong.
2. Design for the worst moment. There’s a wellbeing app built for your worst 2 minutes.
3. Find the smallest reusable unit. One idea runs an entire music marketplace.
4. Constraints sharpen products. A robot releases a new techno track every day, at ₹0.
5. Ship, then harden. Working beats perfect, as long as you’re honest about the gap.

One more thing: I won’t be posting these myself. A small robot I built will, and on the last day I’ll show you how it works.

If you’re hiring for a role like this, or know someone who is, a DM or referral would mean a lot. And if you just enjoy watching things get built, follow along.

title: LifeCycle-OS
post:
Build 1/20: LifeCycle-OS. Enter any brand, get a full lifecycle marketing plan in seconds.
And unlike most AI, it refuses to make up a single price, rating or review.

Lifecycle teams need a constant stream of emails, ads and landing pages for every customer cohort and every market. AI makes them fast. It also invents prices nobody set, ratings nobody earned and reviews nobody wrote. It all reads perfectly, which is exactly why it ships.

The insight: a confident wrong fact costs more than a visible blank.

How it works: LifeCycle-OS benchmarks the brand’s category and designs a complete, ready-to-run lifecycle plan. The platform then turns real customer data into on-brand mailers, ads and landing pages.

The product decisions:
• Missing facts stay missing. The system marks them “DATA REQUIRED BEFORE LAUNCH” instead of guessing.
• One brand’s data can never appear in another brand’s campaign. That’s enforced in code and tested on every change.
• Multi-brand from day one. Any brand onboards, and the whole platform takes on its colours, voice and catalogue.

It started as a simple 3-step tool. It became a platform once I saw that the real problem was trust at scale.

title: The Third Eye
post:
Build 2/20: The Third Eye, a personal AI operating system.
One assistant that works across your tasks, notes, goals, calendar and email, so you stop switching apps.

Tasks in one app, notes in another, email, calendar and goals somewhere else. Your context is everywhere and nowhere.

The insight: you don’t need one more app. You need one assistant that can use the ones you have.

The Third Eye works by voice and camera, takes actions for you, and checks your personal knowledge base before it answers.

The product decisions:
• Four modes (JARVIS, FRIDAY, E.D.I.T.H., ULTRON), so you switch the assistant’s style instead of switching apps.
• A hub, not a silo: 24 tools I built plus 76 linked apps.
• A business model built in: credit packs paid through Razorpay.
• Shipping over perfect architecture. A fuller backend is built and tested, but I didn’t let it hold back a working product.

title: Parwah
post:
Build 3/20: Parwah, a family-care app for Indian families looking after ageing parents.
It ends the WhatsApp line every family knows: “I thought you did.”

“Did anyone book Papa’s blood test?”
“I thought you did.”

Everyone in the family group sees the message. Nobody knows who’s handling it.

The insight: caring for parents is a task problem, not a chat problem.

Parwah (परवाह) answers three questions: what does your parent need, who is handling it, and when is it done?

The product decisions:
• Clear ownership. Every need moves from open, to assigned, to claimed, to done. One tap says “I’m on it”.
• Handing a task back is normal, not a failure. Anyone can reopen a task, and the full history is kept.
• Built for Indian families: siblings in different cities and parents in another, all in one circle.
• Every action checks that the right family member is the one making it.

Apni family ki parwah karein.

title: LoosenUp
post:
Build 4/20: LoosenUp, a stress-relief app built for your worst 2 minutes, not your best 20.
Rate how calm you feel, take a short guided break, and see the difference it made.

Most wellness apps want a sign-up, a 20-minute session and a daily streak. On your worst day, you’ll do none of it. And that’s exactly when you need help.

The insight: design for the worst moment, not the average one.

The product decisions:
• Two minutes, not twenty. A short break matched to what you’re carrying: work, relationships, a low day or sleep.
• Value you can see. Rate how calm you feel before and after, and see your “Calm gain”.
• An SOS button on every screen, even before sign-up: Tele-MANAS 14416, a trusted contact, and emergency 112.
• Distress phrases typed anywhere in the app bring help forward.
• No account needed, works offline, and no app store required.

It’s a wellbeing companion, not medical care, and it says so.

title: Predict Natural Disasters
post:
Build 5/20: Predict Natural Disasters, a live global hazard map built on 8 official data sources.
Its best feature: it grades its own forecasts and tells you when it was wrong.

Most “AI predicts disasters” products make bold forecasts and never check them. In a field where people make real decisions, that’s dangerous.

The problem: disaster data is spread across a dozen agency websites, and nobody knows which forecasts to trust.

What I built: one live map combining USGS, NASA, GDACS, NOAA, EMSC, ReliefWeb and more.

The product decisions:
• Every forecast is accountable. Each one states its evidence, its confidence, and the rule it will be graded by, before the outcome is known.
• If one source goes down, coverage shrinks. The map never goes blank.
• Silence isn’t safety. If no source covers a region, it says “not covered”, never “all clear”.

The trade-off: fewer flashy predictions in exchange for more trust. In high-stakes products, being believed beats being impressive.

title: Edu AI
post:
Build 6/20: Edu AI, an AI-first learning planner for a child’s whole education, from birth to Class 12.
Because today, no app a child uses knows what the last one taught.

From a toddler app to JEE coaching, a child’s education passes through app after app. Each one starts from zero.

The insight: learning is one continuous journey, so the product should track it as one.

Edu AI covers home learning from birth, nursery to Class 12, then competitive and study-abroad tracks.

The product decisions:
• One skill map from age 0 to 18. JEE, NEET, CUET and UPSC tracks branch off it from Class 8-9, instead of starting from scratch.
• Grounded in India’s official curriculum frameworks, across CBSE, ICSE/ISC, NIOS and state boards.
• Zero screen time for children under 3. The product guides parents, not toddlers.
• Data foundations first, because in education the structure is the product.

The bet: whoever holds a learner’s complete history can personalise better than any product that only sees one stage.

title: AI TeleSuite
post:
Build 7/20: AI TeleSuite, an AI toolkit that listens to every sales call so managers can coach.
I built it at The Economic Times, where I scaled Assisted Sales from ₹15L to ₹80L a month.

Sales quality depends on coaching. Coaching depends on listening. And a manager can only hear a handful of calls. The rest go unheard, unscored and uncoached.

The insight: let AI listen to every call, so managers can spend their time coaching.

What it does: call transcription, AI call scoring and pitch assistance, in one toolkit for the Assisted Sales team.

The product decisions:
• Two versions in one product: a full version on paid AI services and a free open-source version. It works on any budget, which makes it easier to adopt.
• Built for internal use, with server-checked PIN access and a lockout, because call data is sensitive.
• Built inside the team that would use it. I didn’t guess at the problem. I lived it every day.

The lesson: the best internal tools come from the person closest to the pain.

title: Hey Yaara
post:
Build 8/20: Hey Yaara, a Hinglish AI voice companion you can call like a friend.
“Yaar, aaj ka din bekaar tha.” Most AI replies like a textbook. Yaara replies like a friend.

Most voice AI is built English-first. Millions of Indians actually talk in Hinglish, and many just want someone to talk to.

The insight: for a voice companion, the experience is the product. And the worst experience is silence.

The product decisions:
• Hinglish by default, built around “calling” Yaara, plus music and games.
• Sign up with a mobile number and PIN, the way Indians already sign up for apps. No email needed.
• Fallbacks everywhere. If the AI model fails, a backup takes over. If the premium voice fails, the phone’s own voice speaks. The call never goes quiet.
• Every call and transcript belongs only to its account, and access is checked on every request.

title: Animind
post:
Build 9/20: Animind, an AI that reads your pet’s state from a 10-second recording.
Not a “pet translator”. It tells you what the sound can actually reveal, and how sure it is.

You can hear that something is wrong with your dog. You just can’t tell what kind of wrong.

“AI pet translators” promise to decode what your animal is saying. But animals don’t use words, so there’s nothing to decode.

The insight: an animal’s sound reliably carries two things: how worked up it is, and whether the sound is distressed or happy. Build on what’s real, not what sounds magical.

What you get: a plain sentence, the measurements behind it, and an honest confidence level.

The product decisions:
• Not a translator, not a diagnosis. The positioning says exactly what it can and can’t do.
• If a recording is too noisy, it says so instead of guessing.
• It compares against what’s normal for the species and for your own animal.
• One engine, four audiences: pet owners, vets, researchers and conservation teams, with plans from free to enterprise.

The lesson: in AI, one of the most valuable features is knowing what you can’t know.

title: TH+ LifeEngine
post:
Build 10/20: TH+ LifeEngine, an AI planner for personalised yoga and food plans.
Ask most AI for a diet plan and you get a paragraph. You can’t track a paragraph.

Personalised yoga and nutrition plans need structure, so an app can schedule, log and adjust them over time.

The insight: AI output only becomes a product feature once it’s structured and checked.

The product decisions:
• Plans follow a fixed format the app can read. Anything else is rejected.
• Two AI steps: one drafts the plan, a second checks it.
• Built from real lists of yoga sequences and foods, not made-up options.
• The optional AI coach sits behind an on/off switch, to keep costs under control.

The rule I took from this and now use everywhere: never let AI output into a product without structure and a second check.

title: Markets Pro
post:
Build 11/20: Markets Pro, a trading research engine for India, the US, China and Russia.
Its demo loses money on purpose, and that’s the most honest thing about it.

Most trading tools show beautiful profit curves. Many quietly cheat: they peek at future prices, ignore taxes, or skip settlement rules. Users trust the curve. Real money pays for the bug.

The insight: the product isn’t trade ideas. It’s numbers you can trust.

What it does: tests two strategies, long-term momentum and short-term swing trades, with each market’s real rules and costs.

The product decisions:
• Real costs for every market: STT, stamp duty and GST in India; regulatory fees in the US; T+1 settlement in China.
• Every calculation is checked against hand-worked answers. One failure blocks the release.
• Audited so no strategy ever sees tomorrow’s prices.
• Paper trading only, with no broker connection. Trust comes before money.

Why the demo loses: it runs on random data. After realistic costs, a strategy should lose there. If it made a profit, that would prove a bug.

title: MuseVibe Studio
post:
Build 12/20: MuseVibe Studio, an AI music studio that turns a one-line idea into a full song.
Most AI music tools give you one text box and hope. This one helps you say what you mean.

Most people know how they want a song to feel. Few know the words for it: genre, tempo, vocal style, studio effects.

The insight: people know the feeling, not the vocabulary. So the product should translate.

What it does: describe your vision in plain words, and MuseVibe fills in every part of the song for you, ready to refine and generate.

The product decisions:
• One line in, every field filled. Write a single sentence and it sets genre, mood, energy, vocals and lyrics.
• AI help on every field, not just the prompt. Each one has Suggest and Enhance, so you can push one detail without starting over.
• Lyrics that respect language. It writes in the language you pick, including natural mixes like Hinglish.
• A single song or a full album, with a matching visual video if you want one.

The lesson: the best AI products don’t just generate. They help people ask for the right thing.

title: Kolab
post:
Build 13/20: Kolab, a two-sided platform for creators and the brands that pay them.
Creators run their whole business in one place. Brands find creators who are verified, not just popular.

Creators run their business across a pile of different apps. Brands still can’t tell which creators are real.

The insight: both sides have the same problem. The tools and the trust live in different places.

What it does: creators plan and schedule content, link every channel, launch a coupon storefront with affiliate codes and get paid. Brands discover verified creators and run commission deals with them.

The product decisions:
• A two-sided business model. Creators subscribe to Basic or Pro plans, and brands partner on commission, so each side pays for the value it gets.
• Verification is the moat. Linked channels are what make a creator trustworthy to a brand.
• Built for India: sign-in by mobile OTP and Aadhaar eKYC is designed in. It’s simulated in the prototype, because real Aadhaar checks need a licensed KYC provider.
• Prototype first. Prove the flow before paying for the expensive parts.

The lesson: in a marketplace, trust is the product. Everything else is features.

title: Shoutout
post:
Build 14/20: Shoutout, one platform for independent musicians to find gigs, collaborators and auditions.
Every request becomes a “Shout” that someone answers, and that one idea runs the whole platform.

An indie musician finds gigs in one place, collaborators in DMs, auditions somewhere else, and gets paid... maybe.

The insight: underneath every interaction is the same action. Someone asks, someone answers.

The product decisions:
• One unit, many uses. 12 types of Shout are set up as configuration, so adding a new one doesn’t mean building a new product.
• One matching engine for every type, so recommendations get better across the whole platform.
• Payments run on proper double-entry accounting, because marketplaces die when payments break.
• Humans review auditions and disputes, where judgement matters.

The principle: find the smallest unit you can reuse, and the platform can grow without being rebuilt.

title: ANCHOR
post:
Build 15/20: ANCHOR, an AI techno artist that releases a new track every single day.
It never sleeps, never burns out, and costs ₹0 to run. It’s a robot I built.

Creators rarely fail for lack of talent. They fail at consistency. I wanted to test whether consistency could be fully automated without breaking platform rules.

Every day, ANCHOR writes a creative brief, generates an industrial techno track, checks its quality, masters it, designs the cover, cuts a YouTube Short, publishes it with AI disclosure, and updates its website.

The product decisions:
• Zero cost as a constraint. Free compute and open-source models shaped everything, and the constraint forced better design.
• Quality gates. Silent or broken tracks never ship.
• Built to respect platform rules. YouTube discourages repetitive mass-produced content, so every release changes the tempo, key, sound, cover and visuals.
• Failure you can see. If a run breaks, the status turns red, and nothing ever posts twice.

Automation is easy. Reliable automation that plays by the rules is the actual product.

title: JobHunt
post:
Build 16/20: JobHunt, a free AI agent that finds real job openings and tailors your resume to each one.
Without ever inventing experience you don’t have.

Job hunting means endless open tabs and one resume sent everywhere.

The insight: the hard part isn’t finding openings. It’s tailoring your application to each one without exaggerating.

What it does: sign in with Google and search once. It pulls real, current openings from free public job boards, and gives you one-click searches on LinkedIn, Indeed, Glassdoor and Upwork. Tap “Tailor & apply” and it writes a resume and cover letter for that exact job.

The product decisions:
• Grounded only in what you give it. It never invents experience.
• Your profile stays in your own browser.
• Free, with no API key and no setup. Google sign-in just keeps usage fair.
• Real listings only, with direct apply links.

The lesson: AI shouldn’t make candidates look like someone else. It should help them show up as themselves, faster.

title: The Watermark Files
post:
Build 17/20: The Watermark Files, an Indian conspiracy-thriller series. 4 books, now on Amazon.
Written with a book engine I built, and published under my own name.

I wanted to test a big question: can one person, with AI, publish a real book series that holds up in the world’s biggest bookstore?

The series: clean, fast-paced thrillers built around old paper. Princely-state deeds, temple inventories, stamp papers and the people who forge them. The lead, Ira Sahni, is a document examiner from Delhi, and every book is a complete case.

Books 1-4: The Palace Writer, The Stamp Vendor, The Second Inventory and The Devpur Deed.

The product decisions:
• A series, not one-offs. A recurring lead builds loyal readers, the way Sherlock Holmes did.
• A niche nobody owns: Indian settings, Indian names, and paper as the clue.
• Quality gates before anything ships: originality and plagiarism checks, plain-English style rules, and a chain of AI models so drafting never stalls.
• Every format, everywhere: Kindle, paperback and hardcover. Book 1 is ₹99 so new readers can try the series.

The lesson: AI doesn’t replace taste. It lets one person run a whole publishing house, as long as the quality gates are real.

title: The Passion Table
post:
Build 18/20: The Passion Table, a daily home-style food service run from neighbourhood kitchens.
Subscribe, order on demand or reserve a table, so nobody at home has to be the one who cooks.

Cooking after work. A cook who didn’t turn up. Another ₹400 delivery you regret by 9 PM.

The problem isn’t food. It’s the daily decision, and the assumption that one person in the house, usually a woman, will handle it.

The insight: restaurant food is a treat. Daily food needs to be home-style, reliable and decided once.

What it does: local “Eating Joints” cook fresh every day, and you choose how the food reaches you.

The product decisions:
• Three ways to eat from one kitchen: a meal subscription, on-demand ordering with live tracking, or a reserved table.
• Choice without the daily decision. Subscribers pick one of three meals each day, and can pause, resume or change any time.
• Home-style, not restaurant-style: food built to be eaten five nights a week.
• The only build on this list with real-world operations, not just software.

title: Airpane
post:
Build 19/20: Airpane, an AR browser that makes any website float in your room.
No headset and no app. Just the phone, laptop and TV you already own.

AR has a hardware problem. Headsets cost more than most phones, and most people will never buy one. But almost everyone has a phone camera and a laptop webcam.

The product decisions:
• Each device does what it’s best at. On a phone, the page stays pinned in your room. On a laptop, the webcam tracks your head so the page looks like a 3D hologram.
• A gesture people already know: pinch, swing and let go to throw a page to your TV. Your phone then becomes the remote.
• No app needed on any device, including iPhones and smart TVs.
• Sites that block embedding open in a cloud browser, which only switches on when it’s enabled, so costs stay in check.

The MVP mindset: prove the “wow” on the cheapest stack, then decide what deserves investment.

title: Portfolio and Anchit LLM

Don’t read my resume. Question it.

title: The robot behind the series
post:
You’ve just read 20 product stories in 20 days. I didn’t publish a single one of them.
Here’s the robot that did, and why I built it.

The problem: builders ship, then go quiet. Writing about your work can take as long as building it, so most projects never get their story told.

The insight: automate the repetitive part, and keep a human exactly where trust lives.

What I built: an autopilot that holds my approved posts in a queue on GitHub and publishes the next one every morning at 9 AM, using LinkedIn’s official API.

The product decisions:
• Publish only. It never likes, comments on others’ posts, messages or connects. Every conversation stays human.
• A content guard checks every post before it goes out. Unfinished placeholders or broken formatting block it.
• I approve every word before it’s queued.
• Built for failure. It never posts twice, a pause switch stops everything, and if a run breaks I get an email and the next day carries on.

It’s built the same way as ANCHOR, my robot that releases a techno track every day.

The lesson: automation shouldn’t replace your voice. It should make sure you actually use it.

That’s the series. If one of these builds sparked an idea, or you’re hiring for a role where product and AI meet, my DMs are open.
